summary: Lists the possible values for IPv4 subnets. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1878.

eli5.summary: A cheat sheet of the sizes into which you can slice an Internet address block.

questions: what are the possible subnet values
subtitle: A reference table of all possible variable-length subnet masks for IPv4 addresses.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to know what subnet masks are valid and what they mean in different notations (hex, CIDR, decimal).
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a complete lookup table of all 32 subnet mask values with their hexadecimal representation, CIDR notation, decimal notation, the number of addresses they provide, and their classful equivalents.
tldr.outcome: This reference was replaced by RFC 1878 as subnetting documentation evolved, but the subnet math has not changed.

facts.label: Address range
facts.value: From 2 to 2,048 million addresses per mask

today: RFC 1860 is obsolete and replaced by RFC 1878. However, the subnet mask values themselves have not changed; the underlying mathematics of IPv4 subnetting remains the same.

sections.title: Variable Length Subnetting
sections.content:
IPv4 addresses can be divided into a network portion and a host (computer) portion using a subnet mask. Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) allows administrators to use different mask sizes on different parts of the network, making efficient use of address space.

Each mask can be written in three ways: as a hexadecimal value (like FF.FF.FF.00), as CIDR notation (like /24, meaning the first 24 bits are the network), or as a dotted decimal (like 255.255.255.0).
sections.eli5: An Internet address is two parts: which network and which computer on that network. A mask says where to split between them. Different masks let you split at different places.

sections.title: The Subnet Table
sections.content:
The RFC lists all 32 possible subnet masks (from /1 to /32), each with its value in all three notations. For example, the /24 mask is written as FF.FF.FF.00 in hex, 255.255.255.0 in decimal, and provides 256 addresses per subnet (though the all-zeros and all-ones addresses are typically reserved).

Each mask also shows its classful equivalent (a class A, B, or C network from the older routing scheme). This helps administrators understand how masks relate to older network structures and the number of usable host addresses in each subnet.
sections.eli5: The table shows: for each mask size, what it looks like in different notations and how many computers can be on a subnet with that mask.

sections.title: Subdividing Networks
sections.content:
The RFC includes examples of how to use VLSM to subdivide common network blocks. For a /16 network (a classful Class B), administrators can add 2 to 14 more bits to the mask and create different numbers of subnets with different numbers of hosts. For a /24 network (a classful Class C), they can add 2 to 6 more bits.

For instance, within a /16 block, using a /24 mask creates 254 subnets, each with 254 hosts; using a /30 mask creates 16,382 subnets, each with 2 hosts (useful for point-to-point links).
sections.eli5: Depending on how you split an address block, you can make many small networks or a few big ones. The table shows the math for common block sizes.

references.text: Fuller, V., Li, T., Yu, J., and K. Varadhan, "Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR): an Address Assignment and Aggregation Strategy", RFC 1519, September 1993.
